title: Joe Louis, Sugar Ray and the numbers racket
summary: Neighborhood memories of Joe Louis at Brewster Center, Sugar Ray, and Detroit's gambling and numbers culture.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Joe Louis had been drafted in... He used to train at the Brewster Center down from where I lived. I used to live on Erskine and Bovian(?), and the Brewster Center was on Hastings one block below Erskine. So it was only one big street, about a block-and-a-half away. That's where Sugar Ray came up, over there in the boxing thing... You know, he had... When he first went in the Army, I used to see him sitting on the steps at the Norwood Hotel down on the (?). He'd sit out on the steps, and he had on his G.I. uniform and everything... Oh, he was really a beautiful man, you know, his complexion and everything. I would just look at him, and he used to just glow, you know. And I remember Sugar Ray used to come down to the Paradise Bowling Alley
before he'd have a fight going, and the guys (?)he'd be with(?) would be betting everybody on the fight. They had all kinds of money.

Detroit was really a sporting town, you know. Everything was going. All kind of hustles were going on. Whatever your game was, it was working, you know. And the numbers were very, very big then, you know, where you put so much on a number and then the number comes out that day, and if you catch it, you win. And there were good odds, 500-to-1. And the numbers man had a lot of money, and they'd be sportin' it up, or just livin' it up... It was really good times. Even though times were a little hard, it was still great times.
